title: Tenth commandment (CCC 2534–2557)
hookLine: envy and greed versus poverty of heart

cards: A friend posts the news: the job came through. The new house. The engagement ring, a close-up of the hand.
And for some people there's a half-second, before typing congratulations, when something in the chest tightens. Not hatred. Nothing anyone would confess out loud.
Just a small, sour question: why them? Stealing, lying, killing are things done. The last commandment, like the ninth, goes underneath the doing, to that half-second.

teach.b: Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house." Wanting good things isn't the sin, the Catechism says; being hungry and wanting bread is fine.
The commandment targets greed without limit, and the wish to get things unjustly, at a neighbor's cost.
Then the quieter relative: envy, which the Catechism calls sadness at the sight of another's goods, and a wish to have them, even unjustly. The tight chest at the good news.

It cites Augustine, who called envy the diabolical sin, and Pope Gregory the Great, who said that from envy come hatred, gossip, slander, and joy at a neighbor's misfortune. What does it offer instead?
Good will, humility, and trust in God's providence.
And it quotes John Chrysostom, who pictured rejoicing in a brother's progress as a way of giving glory to God. Then the heart of it.
Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
The Catechism calls this poverty of heart: detachment from riches, so our hold on things doesn't crowd out God. Not pretending you have nothing; just not being owned by what you have.

And underneath it all is the desire the tenth commandment points toward: the longing to see God. The sour half-second is a hunger aimed at the wrong table. That closes Part Three of the Catechism, how we live.
Part Four is about how we pray.

how: Catholics examine themselves for envy and greed before confession, and the Church teaches good will, humility, trust in providence and detachment from riches as the remedies.

o: a rule only against actual stealing
no greed or envy for what others have
never wanting anything good at all

p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven

s: the tenth commandment says wanting any good thing is a sin
the Catechism says it targets greed without limit and wanting what is a neighbor's, unjustly.
the Catechism treats rejoicing in another's progress as a remedy for envy
quoting John Chrysostom, it pictures that joy as a way of giving glory to God.
poverty of heart means pretending you own nothing
it means detachment: things don't crowd out God.

games.q: a friend's good news gives you a sour half-second. what does the Catechism offer against envy?
o: good will, humility and trust in providence.
work harder until you have more.
games.why: good will, humility and abandonment to God's providence, with joy at a brother's progress.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose good news is a little hard to cheer, a promotion, a baby, a happy family, and picture them on their good day. Notice any tight spot without scolding yourself, then slowly try to want it for them.
If you pray, thank God for their gift by name; if you don't, wish them more of it.

wordCard.voice: The tenth commandment. You shall not covet your neighbor's goods: in Catholic teaching, a guard against greed and envy, and a call to poverty of heart, so that the deepest desire can be for God. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: you shall not covet — the opening of Exodus 20:17.

carryVoice: Your line: enough. Someone else's good takes nothing away from yours. See you in Part Four.
